subject: pathology
title: Glomerular diseases: nephritic and nephrotic patterns

steps.tx: The kidney filter can fail in two broad patterns that every exam stem tests first. **Nephritic syndrome** means inflamed glomeruli that leak blood, so the urine shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts with hypertension and falling filtration. **Nephrotic syndrome** means leaky glomeruli that lose heavy protein, so oedema, low albumin and clotting risk dominate the clinical picture. The syndrome guides the first answer before the biopsy names the disease.
steps.say: The kidney filter can fail through inflammation or through heavy protein leakage in these patients. Inflamed glomeruli bleed and raise blood pressure while leaky glomeruli cause swelling and increase the risk of clotting. You should name the syndrome first because the biopsy result comes later in most questions.

vis.alt: Nephritic versus nephrotic comparison: nephritic means inflamed glomeruli with haematuria, dysmorphic red cells and casts, hypertension and falling filtration; nephrotic means leaky glomeruli with massive proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and thrombosis risk.
vis.caption: Syndrome first, biopsy name second.

steps.tx: **Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis** develops one to three weeks after a skin or throat infection and presents with smoky urine and swelling around the eyes. The complement level C3 falls early and usually recovers within about eight weeks as the inflammation settles. Biopsy shows enlarged hypercellular glomeruli with **subepithelial humps** that represent immune deposits along the capillary wall. Children usually recover fully while adults need closer follow up because recovery is less reliable.
steps.say: This disease follows a streptococcal infection and causes smoky urine with swelling around the eyes. The complement level falls early and then recovers as the inflammation settles over several weeks. Biopsy shows immune deposits that form humps, and children usually recover fully with supportive care.

steps.tx: **IgA nephropathy** is the commonest primary glomerular disease worldwide and presents with visible blood in the urine during or shortly after a throat infection. This synpharyngitic bleeding within a day or two separates it from post streptococcal disease that appears after a longer gap. Immunofluorescence shows dominant **mesangial IgA deposits** with normal complement levels in most patients. A substantial minority progress slowly toward kidney failure over decades, so blood pressure and protein control matter greatly.
steps.say: This disease causes visible bleeding during a sore throat rather than weeks after the infection resolves. Biopsy shows IgA deposits inside the mesangium while complement levels remain normal in most patients. Treatment controls blood pressure and protein loss because a minority progress slowly toward kidney failure.

left.title: Nephritic pattern
points: Dysmorphic haematuria and red cell casts
Examples: post streptococcal, IgA, lupus class IV

right.title: Nephrotic pattern
points: Examples: minimal change, membranous, focal segmental

steps.tx: **Minimal change disease** causes abrupt nephrotic syndrome in children and shows normal light microscopy with effaced foot processes on electron microscopy. It responds dramatically to steroid treatment in most children who present with sudden swelling. **Membranous nephropathy** affects adults and thickens capillary walls with subepithelial spikes, often linked to PLA2R antibodies or an underlying malignancy. **Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis** scars parts of some glomeruli and often resists steroid treatment more strongly.
steps.say: Children with sudden heavy swelling usually have minimal change disease that responds well to steroid treatment. Adults more often develop membranous disease with thickened walls, spikes and antibodies that need malignancy screening. Segmental scarring resists treatment more strongly and carries a worse prognosis for kidney survival.

rows: Child with abrupt nephrotic syndrome, steroid responsive

steps.tx: Rapidly progressive disease fills the Bowman space with **crescents** and destroys filtration over days to weeks, so it needs urgent biopsy and treatment. The causes split into anti glomerular basement membrane disease, immune complex disease and **pauci immune ANCA vasculitis** with very little immune deposit. **Goodpasture syndrome** pairs lung bleeding with linear staining for antibody along the basement membrane. Antibodies to PR3 or MPO guide immunosuppression alongside the biopsy in ANCA associated disease.
steps.say: Crescents fill the Bowman space and destroy kidney function rapidly unless treatment starts very early indeed. Goodpasture disease bleeds into the lungs and shows linear antibody staining along the membrane. ANCA disease deposits almost nothing, so urgent biopsy directs the rescue treatment in every case.

steps.tx: The image shows a glomerulus where a cellular **crescent** fills the Bowman space and compresses the glomerular tuft on one side. The green fluorescence inset supports immune mediated injury inside this rapidly progressive pattern. Recognising a **cellular crescent** matters because filtration can be lost within days without urgent biopsy and treatment. In the exam, crescents on biopsy should trigger immediate thinking about rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and its three immune groups.
steps.say: This image shows a cellular crescent that fills the Bowman space and compresses the normal tuft beside it. The fluorescence inset supports immune injury, and the compressed tuft explains why filtration falls so quickly. You must treat crescents as an emergency because delay causes permanent kidney loss in these patients.
